intro: Why does a new sneaker sell out in a minute and then show up online for double the price? Why does gas cost more in summer? Why does a store with rivals down the street keep cutting prices? Each of these is a market in action. Buyers and sellers meet, and a price comes out of their choices.

In this unit you will read small tables of prices and quantities. You will find the price where buyers and sellers agree. You will tell a shift of a curve from a slide along it. Then you will step inside a business. You will add up revenue, subtract costs and find the profit, using a school store as the example.

By the end, you will be able to explain a real price change in three steps. You will also be able to say why more sellers usually help buyers, what a monopoly is, and why governments watch for businesses that block competition.
bigQuestion: How do buyers, sellers and competition work together to set prices and decide what gets made?

The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the first federal minimum wage
The federal minimum wage rises to $7.25 an hour

when price goes up, the quantity sellers offer goes up, and when price goes down, it goes down
the point where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied
when the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded
when the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied
a shift of the whole demand curve caused by something other than the good's own price
the total money a business takes in; price times quantity sold
revenue minus costs; the money left after all costs are paid
a business the law treats as separate from its owners, who have limited liability
the struggle among sellers to win buyers with better prices, products or service

test.q: The price of a video game drops from $60 to $40, and more people buy it. What is this?
test.why: Only the game's own price changed, so buyers slid along the demand curve.

test.q: Example market: at $6, buyers want 70 and sellers offer 70. What is $6?
test.why: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

test.q: Example: at $9, buyers want 30 and sellers offer 75. What is the result?
test.why: 75 minus 30 equals a surplus of 45 units.

test.q: The cost of flour rises sharply. What happens to the supply of bread?
test.why: Flour is an input cost. Higher input costs shift supply left.

test.q: A popular singer posts a video wearing a brand of hat. What happens to demand for that hat?
test.why: A change in tastes raises demand at every price, a shift right.

test.q: Tickets to a big game sell out instantly at $40 (example price). What does this suggest?
test.why: A sellout is a shortage, which happens when the price is below equilibrium.

test.q: A juice stand sells 60 cups at $2 and has $70 in costs (example numbers). What is its profit?
test.why: Revenue is 60 times $2, or $120. Profit is $120 minus $70, or $50.

test.q: What does the supply curve look like on a graph?
choices: It slopes down from left to right
It slopes up from left to right
test.why: Sellers offer more at higher prices, so the supply curve rises from left to right.

test.q: Which business type is owned by shareholders?
test.why: Shareholders own shares of stock in a corporation.

test.q: Why do more sellers usually mean lower prices?
choices: Sellers compete for the same buyers
test.why: Competition gives each seller a reason to cut prices or improve to win buyers.

test.q: Two rival stores secretly agree to charge the same high price. Which law does this break?
test.why: Price-fixing among rivals is banned by antitrust laws.

test.q: A worker earns $18 an hour for 15 hours (example wage). What does she earn before taxes?
The price of hamburgers, a substitute for hot dogs, rises. What happens to demand for hot dogs?
choices: Supply of hot dogs shifts left
test.why: When a substitute costs more, buyers switch to the other good, so its demand rises.

test.q: A store raises a snack price from $1 to $2 and sales fall from 100 to 40 (example). What happens to revenue?
test.why: Revenue was $1 times 100, or $100. Now it is $2 times 40, or $80.

test.q: What does an entrepreneur get if a risky new business succeeds?
test.why: Profit is the reward for taking the risk of starting a business.

write.prompt: Your school store sells 200 water bottles a week at $1 each (example numbers), and each costs $0.40. A second store opens nearby. Should your store cut its price to $0.80, keep it at $1, or add something new? Use numbers for revenue and profit, and name the trade-offs.
tips: Find revenue (price times quantity) and profit (revenue minus costs) for each choice.
Say how the law of demand affects how many bottles you sell at each price.
Explain what competition from the second store changes.
Name the opportunity cost of the choice you make.
End with a clear decision and one reason it could go wrong.

title: Markets in Action

chapters.title: Supply and Demand on a Graph
chapters.bigQuestion: Who really decides the price of a sneaker, a concert ticket or a gallon of gas?

story.title: The Sneaker Drop
story.kicker: At 10 a.m. a new sneaker goes on sale, and by noon the resale price has doubled.
paragraphs: Maya set three alarms for Saturday. A sports brand was releasing a new sneaker online at 10 a.m. sharp. The store price was $120 (an example price). Maya had saved her birthday money and her dog-walking pay for two months. At 9:58 she was on the website, finger ready over the button.

At 10:00 the page froze. At 10:01 it said SOLD OUT. The company had made only a few thousand pairs in each size. Many more people than that wanted them. Maya refreshed the page again and again. The button stayed gray.

By noon, the same sneakers showed up on a resale app. People who got a pair were selling them for $240 (an example price). That is double the store price. Maya's older brother said, "That's a rip-off." Her friend Jordan said, "No, that's just what people will pay."

Maya did not buy the resale pair. But she kept wondering. Why did the store charge $120 if people would pay $240? Why did the price jump in just two hours? And would it fall again next month? This chapter gives you the tools to answer her questions.
story.think: Who do you agree with, Maya's brother or her friend Jordan? What would make the resale price go down?

lessons.title: The Law of Demand
lessons.mainIdea: When the price of a good goes up, people buy less of it; when the price goes down, they buy more.
reading: Picture a lemonade stand at a summer park. At $3 a cup, the stand sells 100 cups on a hot day. When the owner drops the price to $2, it sells 150 cups. At $1, it sells 220 cups. These are example numbers. The pattern is what matters: a lower price, more cups.

Economists call this the *law of demand*. When the price of a good rises, the amount people want to buy falls. When the price falls, the amount people want to buy rises. The amount people are willing and able to buy at one price is the *quantity demanded*.

Why does this happen? At a higher price, some buyers decide the lemonade is not worth it. Others buy one cup instead of two. Some switch to a water fountain. At a lower price, new buyers join in. Notice the key words: willing AND able. Wanting a thing is not enough. You must also have the money to buy it.

words.d: the rule that when price goes up, the quantity people buy goes down, and when price goes down, it goes up
the amount of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at one certain price

look.title: Movie Night Snacks
look.text: A movie theater sells popcorn for $9 a bag (an example price). One week it runs a special: popcorn for $5. The manager counts the bags sold each night.
look.prompt: Predict what happens to the number of bags sold during the special. Use the law of demand to explain why.

check.q: A store raises the price of a slice of pizza from $3 to $4. What does the law of demand predict?
choices: People will buy the same number of slices
The store will run out of pizza
check.why: The law of demand says a higher price leads to a lower quantity demanded.

check.q: Which buyer is part of demand for a $60 video game?
choices: Sam, who wants it but has only $10
Lee, who has $80 but hates video games
Ana, who wants it and has $70
Rob, who wants it but is not allowed to buy games
check.why: Demand counts buyers who are both willing and able to pay. Only Ana wants the game and has enough money.

check.q: At $2 a stand sells 150 cups. At $3 it sells 100 cups. How many fewer cups sell at the higher price?
check.why: 150 minus 100 equals 50 fewer cups at the higher price.

lessons.title: Reading a Demand Schedule
lessons.mainIdea: A demand schedule is a table that shows how many units buyers want at each price.
reading: Economists often put demand in a small table. The table is called a *demand schedule*. It has two columns. One column lists prices. The other lists the quantity demanded at each price. Here is an example for a school's frozen yogurt cups: at $4, 40 cups; at $3, 70 cups; at $2, 100 cups; at $1, 140 cups.

Read it from top to bottom. As the price falls by $1 each step, the quantity rises. From $4 to $3, quantity goes up by 30 cups. From $2 to $1, it goes up by 40 cups. Every row tells the same story as the law of demand.

You can also turn the table into a graph. Put price on the side (the vertical axis). Put quantity along the bottom (the horizontal axis). Mark a dot for each row and connect the dots. The line slopes down from left to right. That line is the *demand curve*. High prices sit at the top left with small quantities. Low prices sit at the bottom right with big quantities.

words.d: a table that lists the quantity demanded at each price
a graph of the demand schedule; it slopes down from left to right

look.title: Frozen Yogurt Demand (example)
look.cite: Made-up example schedule for a school frozen yogurt sale
look.prompt: How many more cups are demanded at $1 than at $4? Does this table follow the law of demand?

check.q: In the frozen yogurt table, how many cups are demanded at $3?
check.why: Find the $3 row. It shows 70 cups.

check.q: On a graph of demand, which way does the demand curve slope?
choices: It is a straight up-and-down line
check.why: High prices go with small quantities and low prices with large ones, so the curve slopes down from left to right.

check.q: On a supply and demand graph, what goes on the vertical (side) axis?
check.why: By custom, economists put price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.

lessons.title: What Shifts Demand
lessons.mainIdea: A change in income, tastes, related goods or the number of buyers moves the whole demand curve.
reading: Sometimes buyers want more at EVERY price. Say a famous athlete wears a certain backpack in a big game. Before the game, 500 backpacks sold each week at $50 (an example). After the game, 800 sell at that same $50. The price did not change. Something else did. When buyers want more at every price, the demand curve moves to the right. That is an *increase in demand*.

Four main things shift demand. Income: when families earn more, they often buy more of many goods. Tastes: a trend or ad can make a good more popular. Related goods: a *substitute* is a good used in place of another, like a scooter for a bike. If scooters get cheaper, demand for bikes falls. The number of buyers: a new neighborhood brings more customers.

A drop in demand moves the curve to the left. If a news story says a snack is unhealthy, fewer people want it at every price. Buyers' expectations matter too. If people expect a price to rise next week, they may buy more today.

words.d: buyers want more of a good at every price; the demand curve shifts to the right
a good that can be used in place of another, like tea for coffee
the money a person or family earns from work or other sources

look.title: The Rainy Summer
look.text: It rains almost every day in July. A beach town sells sunscreen at the same price as last year, $8 a bottle (an example). Stores sell far fewer bottles. Meanwhile, umbrella sales at the same stores jump.
look.prompt: Did the demand for sunscreen shift left or right? What about umbrellas? Name the cause.

check.q: A new apartment building opens next to a small grocery store. What happens to demand at the store?
choices: It shifts left because of fewer buyers
It shifts right because of more buyers
It does not change because prices stayed the same
check.why: More buyers is one of the shifters of demand. More buyers means more demand at every price, a shift right.

check.q: The price of streaming services falls sharply. Streaming is a substitute for movie tickets. What happens to demand for movie tickets?
choices: The quantity demanded of tickets rises
check.why: When a substitute gets cheaper, people switch to it, so demand for the other good falls and shifts left.

check.q: Which of these would NOT shift the demand curve for pizza?
choices: A popular show makes pizza trendy
The price of pizza itself goes up
The price of tacos, a substitute, goes up
check.why: A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve. It does not shift the curve.

lessons.title: Shift or Slide?
lessons.mainIdea: A change in the good's own price slides along the curve; a change in anything else shifts the curve.
reading: This is the most common mistake in all of economics. Look closely at two events. Event one: a store cuts the price of hot chocolate from $3 to $2, and sales rise from 50 to 80 cups a day (example numbers). Event two: a cold snap hits, and at the same $3 price sales rise from 50 to 90 cups. Both show more cups sold. But they are different.

In event one, only the price changed. Buyers moved to a new point on the SAME demand curve. Economists call this a *change in quantity demanded*. It is a slide along the curve. In event two, the price stayed at $3. The cold weather made buyers want more at every price. That is a *change in demand*. The whole curve shifted right.

Here is a simple test. Ask: did the price of this good change? If yes, it is a slide along the curve. If something else changed, like weather, income or a trend, it is a shift. Never say a price change "shifts demand." A price change never moves the demand curve for that good.

words.d: a move along the demand curve caused only by a change in the good's own price
a shift of the whole demand curve caused by something other than the good's own price

look.title: Two Headlines
look.text: Headline A: "Theater cuts ticket price to $6; crowds grow." Headline B: "Hit movie wins big award; crowds grow at same $10 price." Both use example prices.
look.prompt: Which headline describes a slide along the demand curve and which describes a shift? Explain your test.

check.q: A bakery lowers the price of muffins, and it sells more muffins. What happened?
check.why: Only the muffin price changed, so buyers slid along the same curve. That is a change in quantity demanded.

check.q: A heat wave hits and people buy more fans at the same price. What happened?
choices: Quantity demanded of fans increased because of price
check.why: The price stayed the same and buyers wanted more because of weather, so the whole demand curve shifted right.

check.q: What is the simple test for a shift versus a slide?
choices: Ask if the store made a profit
Ask if the price of the good itself changed
Ask if the weather was good
check.why: If the good's own price changed, it is a slide along the curve. Any other cause is a shift.

lessons.title: The Law of Supply
lessons.mainIdea: When the price of a good goes up, sellers offer more of it; when the price goes down, they offer less.
reading: Now switch sides. Imagine you bake cookies to sell at school. If cookies sell for $0.50 each (an example), you might bake 20. It is not worth much of your time. If they sell for $2 each, you might bake 100. You would give up a movie night to bake. A higher price makes the work worth it.

This is the *law of supply*. When the price of a good rises, sellers offer more of it. When the price falls, they offer less. The amount sellers are willing and able to sell at one price is the *quantity supplied*.

Why? A higher price means more money for each unit. It can cover the extra costs of making more, like more flour, more hours and more oven time. It also pulls new sellers in. If cookies sold for $2, your friends might start baking too. A low price does the opposite. Some sellers decide it is not worth it and stop.

words.d: the rule that when price goes up, the quantity sellers offer goes up, and when price goes down, it goes down
the amount of a good sellers are willing and able to sell at one certain price

look.title: Snow Shoveling
look.text: After a big Chicago snowstorm, neighbors offer $10 to shovel a driveway (an example). Few teens show up. The next storm, neighbors offer $30 a driveway.
look.prompt: What do you predict happens to the number of teens willing to shovel? Which law explains it?

check.q: The price farmers get for corn rises. What does the law of supply predict?
check.why: The law of supply says a higher price leads sellers to offer a larger quantity.

check.q: Which way does a supply curve slope on a graph?
check.why: Higher prices go with larger quantities supplied, so the supply curve rises from left to right.

check.q: Why do new sellers enter a market when the price rises?
choices: They are required to by law
The higher price makes selling worth their costs
The price of the good is falling
check.why: A higher price means more money per unit, which can cover a new seller's costs.

lessons.title: A Supply Schedule
lessons.mainIdea: A supply schedule is a table that shows how many units sellers offer at each price.
reading: Supply fits in a table too. It is called a *supply schedule*. Here is an example for a pottery club that sells mugs at a craft fair: at $4, 20 mugs; at $6, 35 mugs; at $8, 50 mugs; at $10, 60 mugs. As the price rises, the club is willing to make more mugs.

Read the change row by row. From $4 to $6, the club offers 15 more mugs. From $8 to $10, it offers only 10 more. Making extra mugs gets harder as the club runs short of clay, kiln space and members' time. Costs rise, so each price jump brings a smaller increase.

Put the table on a graph with price on the side and quantity on the bottom. The dots rise from left to right. The line through them is the *supply curve*. It slopes the opposite way from the demand curve. That difference matters, because the two curves will cross.

words.d: a table that lists the quantity supplied at each price
a graph of the supply schedule; it slopes up from left to right

look.title: Pottery Club Mugs (example)
look.cite: Made-up example schedule for a school pottery club
look.prompt: How many more mugs does the club offer at $10 than at $4? Does the table follow the law of supply?

check.q: In the pottery table, how many mugs does the club offer at $8?
check.why: Find the $8 row. It shows 50 mugs.

check.q: Using the pottery table, what is the change in quantity supplied from $4 to $10?
check.why: 60 mugs minus 20 mugs equals 40 more mugs.

check.q: How is a supply curve different from a demand curve?
choices: The supply curve is always higher
The supply curve slopes up; the demand curve slopes down
check.why: Sellers offer more at higher prices, so supply slopes up. Buyers want less at higher prices, so demand slopes down.

lessons.title: What Shifts Supply
lessons.mainIdea: A change in costs, technology or the number of sellers moves the whole supply curve.
reading: Supply can shift too. Say a pizza shop makes 300 pizzas a week at $12 each (an example). Then the price of cheese doubles. Each pizza now costs more to make. At the same $12 price, the shop makes only 220 pizzas. When sellers offer less at every price, the supply curve moves left. That is a *decrease in supply*.

Three main things shift supply. *Input costs*: the prices of things used to make a good, like cheese, wages or rent. Higher costs shift supply left. Technology: a faster oven lets the shop make more pizzas for the same cost, so supply shifts right. The number of sellers: when new shops open, supply shifts right.

Nature and events matter too. A drought can shrink a corn crop in Illinois, shifting corn supply left. Remember the same rule as before. A change in the good's OWN price is a slide along the supply curve. Only other causes shift the whole curve.

words.d: sellers offer less of a good at every price; the supply curve shifts to the left
the prices of the things used to make a good, such as materials, wages and rent
new tools and methods that make producing goods easier or cheaper

look.title: The New Machine
look.text: A T-shirt printing shop buys a new machine. It prints a shirt in 1 minute instead of 5. The cost of ink and shirts stays the same.
look.prompt: Which way does the shop's supply curve shift? Name the shifter and explain.

check.q: The wages a bakery pays its workers go up. What happens to the bakery's supply of bread?
check.why: Wages are an input cost. Higher input costs mean sellers offer less at every price, a shift left.

check.q: Ten new food trucks start selling tacos downtown. What happens to the supply of tacos downtown?
choices: The demand for tacos shifts left
check.why: More sellers is a supply shifter. More sellers means more tacos offered at every price.

check.q: Which event is a slide along the supply curve, not a shift?
choices: The price of lumber rises, so builders offer more lumber
A new robot speeds up car making
check.why: Only the price of the good itself changed, so sellers moved along the same curve.

lessons.title: Finding Equilibrium
lessons.mainIdea: The market price settles where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
reading: Put buyers and sellers together. Here is an example market for school spirit T-shirts. At $5: buyers want 90, sellers offer 30. At $10: buyers want 60, sellers offer 60. At $15: buyers want 40, sellers offer 80. Look for the row where the two numbers match. At $10, both sides agree on 60 shirts.

That point is *equilibrium*. The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is the *equilibrium price*. Here it is $10. The amount bought and sold there, 60 shirts, is the equilibrium quantity. On a graph, it is the spot where the demand curve and the supply curve cross.

No one sets this price by a rule. Buyers and sellers find it by trading. If the price is too high, sellers are stuck with extra shirts, so they cut the price. If it is too low, shirts sell out and sellers raise the price. Prices keep adjusting until the two sides balance.

words.d: the point where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied
the price at which buyers want to buy exactly as much as sellers want to sell

look.title: Spirit Shirt Market (example)
look.cite: Made-up example market for school spirit T-shirts
look.prompt: At which price do the two sides match? What would happen at $15?

check.q: Buyers want 200 tickets at $20 and sellers offer 200 tickets at $20. What is $20?
check.why: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At $20, both are 200.

check.q: On a graph, where do you find equilibrium?
choices: Where the supply and demand curves cross
At the top of the demand curve
At the bottom of the supply curve
check.why: Equilibrium is the one point where the two curves meet.

check.q: Example market: at $3, buyers want 50 and sellers offer 50. At $4, buyers want 40 and sellers offer 65. What is the equilibrium quantity?
check.why: The two sides match at $3, where both equal 50 units.

lessons.title: Surplus and Shortage
lessons.mainIdea: A price above equilibrium makes a surplus; a price below equilibrium makes a shortage.
reading: Go back to the spirit shirts. Suppose the club charges $15. Buyers want 40, but the club has 80. That leaves 80 minus 40, or 40 extra shirts. When quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, there is a *surplus*. The fix is a sale. Lower prices draw more buyers and cut how much sellers want to offer.

Now suppose the club charges only $5. Buyers want 90, but the club offers just 30. That leaves 90 minus 30, or 60 shirts missing. When quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied, there is a *shortage*. Lines form and items sell out. Sellers can raise the price, and some buyers drop out.

Both gaps push the price toward equilibrium. A surplus pushes the price down. A shortage pushes the price up. This is Maya's sneaker story. The store price of $120 was below what the market would pay. The shortage sent the resale price up.

words.d: when the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded, so goods are left over
when the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied, so buyers cannot get enough

look.title: Leftover Pumpkins
look.text: On November 1, a farm stand still has 300 pumpkins at $8 each (an example price). Halloween is over, and few people want pumpkins now.
look.prompt: Is this a surplus or a shortage? What will the farm stand likely do to the price, and why?

check.q: Example: at $15, buyers want 40 shirts and sellers offer 80. What is the result?
check.why: Supplied is more than demanded: 80 minus 40 equals a surplus of 40.

check.q: A concert sells out in minutes and fans cannot get tickets. What does this show?
choices: A surplus, so the price was too high
A shortage, so the price was below equilibrium
check.why: More people wanted tickets than there were tickets, which is a shortage caused by a price below equilibrium.

check.q: What usually happens to the price when there is a surplus?
check.why: Sellers with leftover goods lower the price to attract buyers, which moves the market toward equilibrium.

lessons.title: Real Prices, Explained
lessons.mainIdea: To explain a price change, ask which curve shifted, which way, and what that does to the price.
reading: Now you can explain real price changes. Use three steps. First, ask: did demand or supply shift? Second, which way? Third, trace the result. When demand shifts right, price and quantity both rise. When supply shifts left, price rises and quantity falls.

Try gas prices. Gas often costs more in summer, because more families take road trips. That is an increase in demand. If a hurricane shuts down refineries on the Gulf Coast, less gas gets made. That is a decrease in supply. Either shift pushes the price up. When both happen together, prices can jump fast.

Now the video game at launch. On day one, many fans want the game. Demand is high. A year later, most fans already own it, and demand falls. The price often drops. A price change is not magic or greed alone. It is buyers and sellers reacting to a change.

words.d: a move of a whole demand or supply curve to the left or right
any place or system where buyers and sellers trade a good or service

look.title: The Sneaker, Again
look.text: Go back to Maya's sneaker. The company made a few thousand pairs. Many more people wanted them. Resale was $240 by noon. Two months later, the company releases the same shoe again and makes ten times as many pairs.
look.prompt: Which curve shifts when the company makes more pairs? Predict what happens to the resale price and explain.

check.q: A frost destroys much of Florida's orange crop. What happens to the price of orange juice?
choices: It falls, because demand shifts left
It falls, because supply shifts right
It rises, because supply shifts left
check.why: Fewer oranges means less supply at every price. A leftward supply shift raises the price.

check.q: A new study says blueberries are very healthy, and people want more of them. What happens?
check.why: Demand shifts right. Along the upward supply curve, both the price and the quantity sold rise.

check.q: What is the FIRST step in explaining a price change?
choices: Ask whether demand or supply shifted
Draw a picture of the store
check.why: Start by deciding which curve moved; then find the direction and trace the effect on price.

review.q: A cafe raises the price of a smoothie from $5 to $6 and sells fewer smoothies. What is this?
review.why: Only the smoothie price changed, so buyers slid along the demand curve. That is a change in quantity demanded.

review.q: Example market: at $2, buyers want 120 and sellers offer 60. What is the result at $2?
review.why: Demanded is more than supplied: 120 minus 60 equals a shortage of 60.

review.q: Family incomes in a town rise. What happens to the demand for restaurant meals?
review.why: Income is a demand shifter. Higher incomes usually mean more demand for goods like restaurant meals.

review.q: A factory gets a new machine that makes phone cases twice as fast. Which curve shifts, and which way?
review.why: Better technology lowers the cost of making each case, so sellers offer more at every price.

review.q: A store has 500 winter coats left in April. What should happen to the coat price?
choices: It should fall, because there is a surplus
It should rise, because there is a shortage
It should rise, because supply shifted left
review.why: Leftover goods are a surplus, and a surplus pushes the price down toward equilibrium.

review.q: Demand example: at $10, 30 sold; at $8, 45 sold. By how much did quantity demanded change?
review.why: 45 minus 30 equals 15. The lower price led to 15 more units.

review.q: Why does a supply curve slope up?
choices: Buyers want more at high prices
Higher prices cover the extra costs of making more
The government sets it that way
Sellers always sell the same amount
review.why: At a higher price, sellers earn more per unit, which pays for the higher costs of producing more.

review.q: Hot dogs and hot dog buns are used together. The price of hot dogs drops, so people buy more hot dogs. What happens to demand for buns?
review.why: Buns are used with hot dogs. When people buy more hot dogs, they want more buns at every price.

chapters.title: Businesses, Competition and Profit
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it take for a business to earn a profit, and why does competition help buyers?

story.title: The School Store's First Month
story.kicker: The eighth graders opened a school store and found out that selling is the easy part.
paragraphs: In September, Ms. Ortiz's eighth-grade class opened a school store in an old supply closet. They sold pencils, snacks, water and hoodies with the school mascot on them. The principal agreed to lend them the room for $50 a month in rent (an example amount). The class voted on prices and made a big sign.

The first week felt like a win. Students lined up at lunch. The cash box filled with bills and coins. By the end of the month, the store had taken in $900 (an example amount). Some students wanted a pizza party right away. "We're rich!" said Devin.

Then Priya, the class treasurer, spread the receipts on a desk. The snacks had cost $300. The hoodies had cost $450. Rent was $50. Printing the sign had cost $25. And 12 hoodies were still sitting in a box, unsold, in sizes nobody wanted.

Priya did the math out loud. "We brought in $900. We spent $825. We kept $75." The room got quiet. Then someone asked the hard questions. Should they raise prices? Order fewer hoodies? What if the eighth graders down the hall opened their own store? This chapter follows those questions.
story.think: Did the store really make money in its first month? What would you change for month two?

lessons.title: Revenue and Costs
lessons.mainIdea: Revenue is the money a business takes in; costs are the money it spends to run.
reading: Start with the school store's cash box. Every sale adds money. Say the store sells 150 bags of chips at $1 each and 40 bottles of water at $1.50 each (example prices). Chips bring in 150 times $1, or $150. Water brings in 40 times $1.50, or $60. Together that is $210.

The money a business takes in from sales is its *revenue*. To find it, multiply the price by the number sold, then add up every product. Revenue is NOT the same as the money the business gets to keep. That is a common mistake, and it was Devin's mistake in the story.

A business also pays *costs*. Costs are the money spent to make and sell its goods. The store pays for the chips it buys to resell, the rent for the room and the paint for the sign. Some costs stay the same no matter how much you sell, like rent. These are *fixed costs*. Others grow with each sale, like the chips themselves. These are variable costs.

words.d: the total money a business takes in from sales; price times quantity sold
the money a business spends to make and sell its goods or services
costs that stay the same no matter how much a business sells, like rent

look.title: School Store Sales, One Week (example)
look.cite: Made-up example sales for a middle school store
look.prompt: What was the store's total revenue this week? Which product brought in the most?

check.q: A car wash washes 40 cars at $8 each (example price). What is its revenue?
check.why: Revenue is price times quantity: 40 times $8 equals $320.

check.q: Which of these is a fixed cost for a food truck?
choices: The ground beef for each taco
The napkins given with each order
check.why: The permit costs the same whether the truck sells 10 tacos or 1,000. The others rise with each sale.

check.q: Devin sees $900 in the cash box and says the store is rich. What mistake is he making?
choices: He is confusing revenue with profit
He is confusing supply with demand
He forgot the price of hoodies
check.why: $900 is revenue. The store must still subtract its costs to find what it keeps.

lessons.title: Profit and Loss
lessons.mainIdea: Profit is revenue minus costs; if costs are bigger than revenue, the business has a loss.
reading: Now use Priya's receipts. The store brought in $900. Its costs were $300 for snacks, $450 for hoodies, $50 for rent and $25 for the sign. Add the costs: 300 plus 450 plus 50 plus 25 equals $825. Then subtract: $900 minus $825 equals $75.

That $75 is the store's *profit*. Profit is what is left after a business pays all its costs. The rule is short: profit equals revenue minus costs. If the costs had been $950, the store would have a *loss* of $50. A loss means the business spent more than it took in.

Profit sends a signal. A big profit tells other sellers that people want this product, so more may enter the market. A loss tells a business to change something: cut costs, change prices or sell something else. Profit is also the reward owners get for taking a risk with their money and time.

words.d: the money left after a business pays all its costs; revenue minus costs
what happens when a business's costs are greater than its revenue

look.title: Month Two Choices
look.text: For month two, the school store has two ideas. Plan A: stop selling hoodies, which cost $450 and brought in only $360 (example amounts). Plan B: keep hoodies but order only the sizes that sold.
look.prompt: Did the hoodies earn a profit or a loss in month one? Which plan would you pick, and what do you give up?

check.q: A lemonade stand takes in $120 and spends $45 on lemons, sugar and cups (example amounts). What is its profit?
check.why: Profit equals revenue minus costs: $120 minus $45 equals $75.

check.q: A bakery has revenue of $2,000 and costs of $2,300 in one month (example amounts). What happened?
check.why: Costs are bigger than revenue. $2,300 minus $2,000 equals a $300 loss.

check.q: Many new shops open after one ice cream shop earns big profits. Why?
choices: Ice cream got cheaper to make
The profit signaled that people want ice cream
The first shop asked for help
check.why: High profits signal strong demand, which draws new sellers into the market.

lessons.title: Pricing for Profit
lessons.mainIdea: A higher price does not always mean more revenue, because buyers purchase fewer units.
reading: Should the store just raise prices? Try it with example numbers. At $1 a bag, the store sells 150 bags of chips, so revenue is $150. At $2 a bag, students buy only 60 bags, so revenue is 60 times $2, or $120. The higher price brought in LESS money. Many students bought cookies or brought chips from home.

Remember the law of demand. When the price goes up, the quantity demanded goes down. A business must think about both parts of revenue: price and quantity. Raising the price helps only if sales do not fall too much.

How much buyers react depends on the good. If there are many substitutes, buyers switch fast. If there are few substitutes, like water on a hot field day, buyers react less. Businesses test prices, watch what sells and adjust. That is why stores run sales and try new prices.

words.d: the amount of money a buyer pays for one unit of a good or service
a good that can be used in place of another, like cookies in place of chips

look.title: Chip Price Test (example)
look.cite: Made-up example price test for a school store
look.prompt: Find the revenue at each price (price times bags). Which prices bring in the most revenue?

check.q: Using the chip table, what is the revenue at $1.50 a bag?
check.why: 100 bags times $1.50 equals $150.

check.q: Using the chip table, which price brings in the LEAST revenue?
check.why: $0.50 times 200 is $100; $1.00 gives $150; $1.50 gives $150; $2.00 gives $120. $100 is the least.

check.q: Why can raising a price lower a store's revenue?
choices: Buyers purchase fewer units at the higher price
check.why: Revenue is price times quantity. If quantity falls enough, revenue drops even at a higher price.

lessons.title: One Owner or Partners
lessons.mainIdea: A sole proprietorship has one owner; a partnership has two or more who share the business.
reading: Think of a neighbor who runs a lawn-mowing business alone. She owns it all. She makes every choice and keeps every dollar of profit. This is a *sole proprietorship*, a business owned by one person. It is the most common kind of business in the United States, and it is easy to start.

But there is a big risk. If the business owes money it cannot pay, the owner may have to pay it from her own savings. This is called unlimited liability. Liability means legal responsibility for debts. Her car or savings could be at risk if the business fails.

Now picture two friends who open a bike repair shop. They each put in money and share the work and the profit. This is a *partnership*, a business owned by two or more people. Partners can pool money and skills. But they must agree on choices, and in a general partnership each partner can be responsible for the business's debts.

words.d: a business owned and run by one person, who keeps the profits and is responsible for the debts
a business owned by two or more people who share the work, profits and debts
legal responsibility for a business's debts

look.title: Going It Alone?
look.text: Jaden bakes great cakes and wants to sell them. His cousin Rosa is good with numbers and has $2,000 saved (an example amount). She offers to be his partner and split the profit half and half.
look.prompt: What would Jaden gain from a partnership? What would he give up? Would you take the deal?

check.q: A dog-walker runs her business alone and keeps all the profit. What kind of business is it?
check.why: A business owned by one person is a sole proprietorship.

check.q: What is one big risk of a sole proprietorship?
choices: The owner may have to pay business debts from personal savings
check.why: Sole proprietors have unlimited liability, so personal money can be used to pay business debts.

check.q: Why might two people form a partnership?
choices: To combine their money and skills
To keep all the profit for one person
check.why: Partners pool money, skills and work. They still share risk and profit.

lessons.title: Corporations
lessons.mainIdea: A corporation is a business that is its own legal unit, owned by shareholders who risk only what they invested.
reading: Big companies that make phones, cars or cereal are usually corporations. A *corporation* is a business that the law treats as separate from its owners. It can own property, sign contracts and borrow money in its own name.

The owners of a corporation are its *shareholders*. They own small pieces of the company called shares, or stock. Say a company has 1,000 shares and you buy 10 (an example). You own 10 divided by 1,000, or 1% of the company. If it earns a profit, it may pay part of it to shareholders.

The big advantage is limited liability. If the corporation fails, shareholders can lose the money they put in, but not their homes or savings. Selling shares also raises large amounts of money. The trade-offs: corporations cost more to set up, must follow more rules and file more reports, and owners may have little say in daily choices.

words.d: a business the law treats as separate from its owners, able to own property and borrow in its own name
a person who owns shares, or stock, in a corporation
owners can lose only the money they invested, not their personal property

look.title: Which Type Fits? (example counts)
look.cite: Made-up example: 10 businesses on one neighborhood street
look.prompt: What percent of the businesses on this example street are sole proprietorships? Why might small shops choose that type?

check.q: A company has 2,000 shares. You own 20 (example numbers). What percent of the company do you own?
check.why: 20 divided by 2,000 equals 0.01, which is 1%.

check.q: What is the main advantage of limited liability for shareholders?
choices: They can lose only the money they invested
check.why: Limited liability protects shareholders' personal property if the business fails.

check.q: Which is a trade-off of forming a corporation?
choices: The owner is personally responsible for all debts
It costs more to set up and has more rules
It can have only one owner
check.why: Corporations gain limited liability and easier fundraising, but they face higher setup costs and more rules.

lessons.title: Why More Sellers Help Buyers
lessons.mainIdea: Competition among many sellers usually pushes prices down and quality up.
reading: Back to the story. The eighth graders down the hall open a second store. Right away, things change. The first store sold water for $1.50 (an example price). The new store sells it for $1.25. Students walk down the hall to save a quarter. Soon the first store cuts its price to $1.25 too.

This is *competition*: sellers trying to win the same buyers. When buyers can choose, each seller has a reason to offer lower prices, better products or faster service. A store that charges too much or treats customers poorly loses sales to its rival.

Competition also pushes new ideas. The first store starts selling fruit cups, which the other store does not have. Competition is not always comfortable for sellers. Some lose money and close. But for buyers, more sellers usually mean lower prices and more choices.

words.d: the struggle among sellers to attract buyers by offering better prices, products or service
another business that tries to sell to the same buyers

look.title: Adam Smith on Self-Interest
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776, Book I, Chapter 2
look.prompt: Benevolence means kindness. In your own words, why does the baker sell you bread? How does competition turn a seller's self-interest into good deals for buyers?

check.q: A town has one pizza shop. Three more open nearby. What will most likely happen to pizza prices?
choices: They will stay the same forever
check.why: More sellers compete for the same buyers, which usually pushes prices down.

check.q: Which is a way businesses compete besides price?
choices: Charging more for the same thing
Offering better quality or new products
check.why: Sellers can win buyers with quality, new products or better service, not only lower prices.

check.q: What did Adam Smith mean about the butcher and baker?
choices: They sell to us because it serves their own interest
They give food away for free
check.why: Smith argued that sellers serve buyers because it helps themselves, and trade benefits both sides.

lessons.title: When There Is Only One Seller
lessons.mainIdea: A monopoly is a market with only one seller, which can charge more and has less reason to improve.
reading: Now imagine the school allows only ONE store. There is no other place to buy water at lunch. The store raises water from $1.25 to $2 (example prices). Some students skip water, but many still buy it. They have no other choice nearby.

A market with only one seller of a good that has no close substitutes is a *monopoly*. A monopoly can often charge higher prices and sell less than a competitive market would. With no rival, it also has less reason to improve quality or service.

Some monopolies happen for good reasons. A company may hold a *patent*, a right from the government to be the only seller of a new invention for a set time. That reward encourages people to invent. A town often has one water system, because building two sets of pipes would waste money. Governments often set rules on the prices such services can charge.

words.d: a market with only one seller of a good that has no close substitutes
a government grant that gives an inventor the only right to make and sell an invention for a set time

look.title: The Only Gas Station
look.text: A small town far from any highway has one gas station. The nearest other station is 40 miles away. The owner charges 50 cents a gallon more than stations in the city (an example).
look.prompt: Why can this owner charge more? What might happen if a second station opened in town?

check.q: Which is the best example of a monopoly?
choices: Ten coffee shops on one street
Three phone brands in a store
The only company allowed to sell water service in a town
check.why: A monopoly has only one seller with no close substitutes, like a single town water service.

check.q: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly usually has:
choices: higher prices and less reason to improve
check.why: With no rivals, a monopoly can charge more and faces less pressure to improve.

check.q: Why does the government give patents, which create short-term monopolies?
choices: To help buyers pay less right away
check.why: A patent lets an inventor be the only seller for a set time, which rewards the work of inventing.

lessons.title: Keeping Markets Fair
lessons.mainIdea: Governments use antitrust laws to stop businesses from blocking competition.
reading: Sometimes businesses try to escape competition on purpose. Say the two school stores secretly agree to both charge $2 for water instead of $1.25 (example prices). Neither one loses customers, and students pay more. An agreement like this among rivals to fix prices hurts buyers.

Adam Smith warned about this back in 1776. The United States passed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890. *Antitrust laws* are laws that ban price-fixing and other ways of blocking competition. The government can also study a merger. A *merger* is when two companies join into one. If it would leave buyers with too few choices, the government can try to stop it in court.

Economists debate how much to step in. Some say big firms can be efficient and lower costs, so the government should act only when buyers are clearly harmed. Others say giant firms can crush new rivals and should be watched more closely. Both sides agree that price-fixing among rivals hurts buyers.

words.d: laws that ban price-fixing and other actions that block competition
when two companies join together to form one company
a secret agreement among rival sellers to charge the same high price

look.title: Adam Smith's Warning
look.text: People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776, Book I, Chapter 10
look.prompt: A conspiracy is a secret plan; a contrivance is a trick. What was Smith worried sellers might do when they meet? Which law today tries to stop it?

check.q: Two rival airlines secretly agree to raise fares on the same day. What is this called?
check.why: Rivals agreeing on prices is price-fixing, which antitrust laws ban.

check.q: In what year did the United States pass the Sherman Antitrust Act?
check.why: The Sherman Antitrust Act became law in 1890.

check.q: Why might the government try to block a merger of the two biggest companies in a market?
choices: Buyers could be left with too few choices
check.why: Antitrust officials act when a merger would cut competition and hurt buyers.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurs Take the Risk
lessons.mainIdea: An entrepreneur starts a business, takes on risk and earns profit as the reward if it works.
reading: Every business starts with someone willing to try. An *entrepreneur* is a person who starts a business and takes on the risk. Say a teen named Leo spends $200 of his savings on a used snow blower (an example). If it snows a lot, he earns $600 clearing driveways. If it barely snows, he might earn only $100 and lose money.

That chance of losing is *risk*. The possible profit is the reward. Leo's profit in the snowy winter would be $600 minus $200, or $400. In the dry winter, $100 minus $200 is a loss of $100. Entrepreneurs start businesses because they believe the reward is worth the risk.

Starting a business also has an opportunity cost. Leo could have kept his $200 or spent his time on something else. Many new businesses fail. But entrepreneurs who succeed bring new products and jobs. They spot a need, like shoveled driveways on a busy street, and fill it.

words.d: a person who starts a new business and takes on the risk of losing money
the chance of losing money or something of value
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: The Phone Case Idea
look.text: Aisha wants to design and sell phone cases online. She needs $300 for supplies (an example). She could instead use that $300 for a summer camp she really wants.
look.prompt: What is Aisha's risk? What is her opportunity cost? What would help her decide?

check.q: Leo spends $200 on a snow blower and earns $600. What is his profit?
check.why: Profit equals revenue minus costs: $600 minus $200 equals $400.

check.q: What is the reward an entrepreneur hopes for in exchange for risk?
check.why: Profit is the reward for taking on the risk of starting a business.

check.q: Aisha spends her $300 on phone case supplies instead of camp. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: The summer camp she gave up
check.why: Opportunity cost is the next-best choice given up, which is the camp.

lessons.title: A Plan for the School Store
lessons.mainIdea: A business plan lists what you will sell, to whom, at what price, and how you expect to earn a profit.
reading: Before month two, Ms. Ortiz's class writes a *business plan*. A business plan is a written guide to how a business will work and make money. Theirs answers five questions. What will we sell? Who will buy it? What will we charge? What will it cost? How much profit do we expect?

The class uses its month-one numbers. They expect to sell 300 snacks at $1.25 each, or $375 (example numbers). The snacks cost $0.60 each, so 300 cost $180. Rent stays $50. Expected profit on snacks: $375 minus $180 minus $50 equals $145. They decide to order hoodies only after taking pre-orders, so none are left over.

A plan also names the competition, in this case the other store, and how to stand out. The class plans to sell fruit cups and open five minutes earlier. A plan does not guarantee success. But it makes owners check their numbers before they spend real money.

words.d: a written guide that explains what a business will sell, to whom, at what price, and how it expects to earn a profit
the total money a business takes in from sales; price times quantity sold

look.title: Month Two Plan (example)
look.cite: Made-up example business plan for a school store
look.prompt: Check the math: does revenue minus both costs equal the expected profit? What would profit be if rent rose to $80?

check.q: In the example plan, what would the expected profit be if rent rose from $50 to $80?
check.why: $375 minus $180 minus $80 equals $115.

check.q: Why did the class decide to take pre-orders for hoodies?
choices: To avoid leftover hoodies, a surplus
check.why: Pre-orders match the number made to the number wanted, so the store avoids unsold stock.

check.q: Which question does a business plan NOT need to answer?
choices: What is every student's favorite color?
check.why: A plan covers what to sell, to whom, the price, the costs and expected profit, not unrelated facts.

lessons.title: Workers, Wages and Unions
lessons.mainIdea: Wages are set mostly by the supply of and demand for workers; unions let workers bargain as a group.
reading: The school store needs cashiers. Workers are part of a market too. A *wage* is the payment a worker earns for work, often counted per hour. Say a shop pays $15 an hour for 20 hours a week (an example). The worker earns 15 times 20, or $300 a week before taxes.

Wages follow supply and demand. When many people can do a job and few businesses need it, wages tend to be lower. When a job needs rare skills, like a nurse or electrician, and many employers need them, wages tend to be higher. Training and education often raise what a worker can earn.

A *labor union* is a group of workers who join together to bargain with an employer about wages, hours and safety. Bargaining as a group is called collective bargaining. Supporters say unions give workers a stronger voice and better pay. Critics say they can raise costs, which may lead firms to hire fewer workers. Economists study and debate both effects, including the effects of the federal minimum wage, which has been $7.25 an hour since 2009.

words.d: the payment a worker earns for work, often counted per hour
a group of workers who join together to bargain with employers about pay, hours and working conditions
talks between a union and an employer to agree on wages and working conditions

look.title: Two Job Offers
look.text: Carlos gets two summer job offers (example wages). A grocery store pays $14 an hour for 25 hours a week. A lifeguard job pays $17 an hour for 20 hours, but he must first take a certification class.
look.prompt: Which job pays more per week? Why might the lifeguard job pay a higher hourly wage?

check.q: A worker earns $16 an hour and works 25 hours (example wage). What does she earn before taxes?
check.why: 16 times 25 equals $400.

check.q: Why do jobs that need rare skills usually pay higher wages?
choices: Few workers can do them, and many employers need them
check.why: A small supply of skilled workers and a high demand for them push wages up.

check.q: What is one argument critics make about unions?
choices: Higher costs may lead firms to hire fewer workers
Unions are the same as monopolies on goods
check.why: Critics argue that union-won wage gains raise costs, which can reduce hiring. Supporters stress better pay and voice.

review.q: A school store takes in $500 and has $380 in costs (example amounts). What is its profit?
review.why: Profit equals revenue minus costs: $500 minus $380 equals $120.

review.q: Which business type gives owners limited liability?
choices: A lemonade stand run by one person
review.why: Corporation shareholders can lose only what they invested.

review.q: A shop sells 80 caps at $12 each (example price). What is its revenue?
review.why: Revenue is price times quantity: 80 times $12 equals $960.

review.q: Only one company sells electricity in a region, and there is no close substitute. What is this market?
review.why: A single seller with no close substitutes is a monopoly.

review.q: A second school store opens and cuts the price of water. What does this show?
review.why: A rival seller competing for buyers pushes prices down.

review.q: Which is a fixed cost for the school store?
choices: The monthly rent for the room
The chips it buys to resell
review.why: Rent stays the same no matter how much the store sells.

review.q: What is the main purpose of antitrust laws?
choices: To protect competition and stop price-fixing
review.why: Antitrust laws ban actions like price-fixing that block competition and hurt buyers.

review.q: An entrepreneur spends $500 on supplies and earns $350 in sales (example amounts). What is the result?
review.why: Costs are bigger than revenue: $500 minus $350 equals a loss of $150.
